In [[vector calculus]], a '''Beltrami vector field''', named after [[Eugenio Beltrami]], is a [[vector field]] in three dimensions that is parallel to its own [[curl (mathematics)|curl]].  That is, '''F''' is a Beltrami vector field provided that
<math display="block">\mathbf{F}\times (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})=0.</math>

Thus <math>\mathbf{F}</math> and <math>\nabla\times\mathbf{F}</math> are parallel vectors in other words, <math>\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \lambda \mathbf{F}</math>.

If <math>\mathbf{F}</math> is solenoidal - that is, if <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0</math> such as for an incompressible fluid or a magnetic field, the identity  <math>\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \equiv -\nabla^2 \mathbf{F} + \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})</math> becomes <math>\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \equiv -\nabla^2 \mathbf{F}</math> and this leads to
<math display="block">-\nabla^2 \mathbf{F} = \nabla \times(\lambda \mathbf{F})</math>
and if we further assume that <math>\lambda</math> is a constant, we arrive at the simple form
<math display="block">\nabla^2 \mathbf{F} = -\lambda^2 \mathbf{F}.</math>

Beltrami vector fields with nonzero curl correspond to Euclidean [[contact form]]s in three dimensions.

The vector field
<math display="block">\mathbf{F} = -\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+z^2}}\mathbf{i} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+z^2}}\mathbf{j}</math>
is a multiple of the standard contact structure −''z'''''i'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;'''j''', and furnishes an example of a Beltrami vector field.

== Beltrami fields and fluid mechanics==
Beltrami fields with a constant proportionality factor are a distinct category of vector fields that act as eigenfunctions of the curl operator. In essence, they are functions that map points in a [[three-dimensional space]], either in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> (Euclidean space) or on a flat torus <math>\mathbb{T}^3</math>, to other points in the same space. Mathematically, this can be represented as:

<math>u: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3</math> (for Euclidean space) or <math>u: \mathbb{T}^3 \to \mathbb{T}^3</math> (for the flat torus).

These vector fields are unique due to the special relationship between the curl of the vector field <math>u</math> and the field itself. This relationship can be expressed using the following equation:

<math>\nabla \times u = \lambda u</math>

In this equation, <math>\lambda</math> is a non-zero constant, which indicates that the curl of the vector field <math>u</math> is proportional to the field itself.

Beltrami fields are relevant in fluid dynamics, as they offer a classical family of stationary solutions to the Euler equation in three dimensions.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-74278-2 |title=Topological Methods in Hydrodynamics |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-74278-2}}</ref> The [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]] describe the motion of an ideal, incompressible fluid and can be written as a system of two equations:

<math>
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} + (u \cdot \nabla)u = -\nabla p, \\
\nabla \cdot u = 0.
\end{cases}
</math>
For stationary flows, where the velocity field <math>u</math> does not change with time, i.e. <math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=0 </math>, we can introduce the [[Bernoulli's principle|Bernoulli]] function, <math>B := p + \frac{1}{2}\lVert u \rVert^2</math>, and the [[Vorticity equation|vorticity]], <math>\omega := \nabla \times u</math>. These new variables simplify the Euler equations into the following system:

<math>
\begin{cases}
u \times \omega = \nabla B, \\
\nabla \cdot u = 0.
\end{cases}
</math>
The simplification is possible due to [[Vector calculus identities#Vector dot Del Operator|a vector identity]], which relates the convective term <math>(u \cdot \nabla)u</math> to the gradient of the kinetic energy and the [[cross product]] of the velocity field and its curl:

<math>(u \cdot \nabla)u = \frac{1}{2}\nabla \lVert u \rVert^2 - u \times (\nabla \times u)</math>

When the Bernoulli function <math>B</math> is constant, Beltrami fields become valid solutions to the simplified Euler equations. Note that we do not need the proportionality factor to be constant for the proof to work.

=== Beltrami fields and complexity in fluid mechanics ===
Beltrami fields have a close connection to Lagrangian turbulence, as shown by [[Vladimir Arnold|V.I. Arnold]]'s work on stationary Euler flows.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Arnold |first=Vladimir |date=1966 |title=Sur la géométrie différentielle des groupes de Lie de dimension infinie et ses applications à l'hydrodynamique des fluides parfaits |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/AIF_1966__16_1_319_0/ |journal=Annales de l'Institut Fourier |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=319–361 |doi=10.5802/aif.233 |issn=1777-5310|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Arnold |first=Vladimir I. |chapter=Sur la topologie des écoulements stationnaires des fluides parfaits |date=2014 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-31031-7_3 |title=Vladimir I. Arnold - Collected Works: Hydrodynamics, Bifurcation Theory, and Algebraic Geometry 1965-1972 |pages=15–18 |editor-last=Arnold |editor-first=Vladimir I. |access-date=2023-05-01 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-31031-7_3 |isbn=978-3-642-31031-7 |editor2-last=Givental |editor2-first=Alexander B. |editor3-last=Khesin |editor3-first=Boris A. |editor4-last=Varchenko |editor4-first=Alexander N.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==== Arnold's "conjecture" ====
Arnold's quote from his aforementioned work highlights the probable complicated topology of the streamlines in Beltrami fields, drawing parallels with celestial mechanics:

<blockquote>
Il est probable que les écoulements tels que rot <math>\nu =\lambda\nu</math>, <math>\lambda=Cte</math>, ont des lignes de courant à la topologie compliquée. De telles complications interviennent en mécanique céleste. La topologie des lignes de courant des écoulements stationnaires des fluides visqueux peut être semblable à celle de mécanique céleste.
</blockquote>

==== Proposed solutions ====

A recent paper<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Enciso |first=Alberto |last2=Peralta-Salas |first2=Daniel |last3=Romaniega |first3=Álvaro |date=2023 |title=Beltrami fields exhibit knots and chaos almost surely |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-sigma/article/beltrami-fields-exhibit-knots-and-chaos-almost-surely/D49335EF3C9FD37319BB9BE7F7DBD380 |journal=Forum of Mathematics, Sigma |language=en |volume=11|doi=10.1017/fms.2023.52 |issn=2050-5094|doi-access=free |arxiv=2006.15033 }}</ref> demonstrates that Beltrami fields exhibit chaotic regions and [[invariant tori]] of complex topologies [[with high probability]]. The analysis includes asymptotic bounds for the number of [[Horseshoe map|horseshoes]], zeros, and knotted invariant tori, alongside [[Orbit (dynamics)|periodic trajectories]] in [[Gaussian random field|Gaussian random]] Beltrami fields.
